title: 4 · Arrays & ArrayList (Deep Dive)
learn:
The story: a row of lockers

Hallway lockers are numbered from 0, all the same size, and the row cannot grow. That is an array: a fixed-size collection of the same type, indexed from 0 to length-1. It is an object (reference type) even when it holds primitives.

Creating arrays

int[] marks = new int[5]; makes 5 slots filled with defaults (0 for numbers, false for boolean, null for objects). int[] marks = {90, 45, 77}; fills it directly. marks.length is a field, no brackets. Out of range access throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

Everyday array code

Loop with a normal for when you need the index, for-each when you only need values. Arrays.sort(a) sorts in place and Arrays.toString(a) prints it (import java.util.Arrays). Copy with Arrays.copyOf; writing b = a copies only the reference, so both names share one array.

Array pros and cons

Pros: very fast index access, memory efficient, simple. Cons: fixed size, only one type, inserting or deleting in the middle means shifting elements by hand.

2D arrays

An array of arrays: int[][] g = {{1,2,3},{4,5,6}}; g[1][2] is 6 (row first, then column). g.length is the rows, g[0].length the columns. Process with nested loops.

ArrayList: the stretchy locker row

An ArrayList grows and shrinks automatically. ArrayList list = new ArrayList<>(); The type in angle brackets limits what it holds. Core methods: add(x), get(i), set(i, x), remove(i), size(), contains(x), isEmpty().

Why Integer, not int?

Collections hold objects only. Each primitive has a wrapper: int/Integer, double/Double, char/Character, boolean/Boolean, long/Long. Autoboxing converts int to Integer automatically; unboxing converts back. Trap: on ArrayList, remove(1) removes the item at index 1, not the value 1.

Array vs ArrayList

Array: fixed size, primitives or objects, length, a[i]. ArrayList: dynamic, objects only, size(), get(i), needs import java.util.ArrayList. Exam tables love this.
